text:
I. The Birth of the New Order and the Annihilation of the Left (1965–1967)

Just after midnight on October 1, 1965, military detachments drawn largely from the Cakrabirawa Presidential Guard, operating under a clandestine group calling itself the 30 September Movement (G30S), fanned out across Jakarta to abduct seven of the Indonesian Army's senior generals. The raids were swift and lethal. Army commander Lieutenant General Ahmad Yani was shot dead in his living room in front of his children, along with Brigadier General D.I. Panjaitan and Major General M.T. Haryono at their homes. Major Generals Suprapto and S. Parman, alongside Brigadier General Sutoyo Siswomiharjo, were seized alive and thrown into waiting army trucks. The seventh target, Defense Minister General Abdul Haris Nasution, vaulted over his garden wall in the dark with a broken ankle as bullets tore through his bedroom, mortally wounding his five-year-old daughter, Ade Irma Suryani, while his young adjutant, Lieutenant Pierre Tendean, was taken in his stead. All six abductees were driven to a rubber plantation on the southern edge of Halim Air Base known as Lubang Buaya—Crocodile Hole—where those still breathing were executed and dumped into an abandoned eleven-meter well.

Within twenty-four hours, the poorly coordinated movement collapsed. Major General Suharto, commander of the Army Strategic Reserve (Kostrad), took control of the capital before the plotters had even finished reading their decrees over state radio. What followed was a masterclass in psychological warfare. Army-controlled newspapers and radio broadcasts flooded the country with lurid, fabricated accounts claiming that the generals had been tortured, castrated, and had their eyes gouged out by women of Gerwani, an organization linked to the Indonesian Communist Party (PKI), during a ritualistic dance at Lubang Buaya. Even though the official forensic autopsies—ordered by Suharto himself—quietly confirmed the victims had died of ordinary gunshot wounds and blunt trauma with every organ intact, the lie did exactly what it was engineered to do: it whipped the nation into an apocalyptic frenzy.

Over the next six months, across Central and East Java, Bali, and North Sumatra, the army's RPKAD paracommandoes under Colonel Sarwo Edhie Wibowo armed, trained, and unleashed civilian militias, religious youth wings, and local vigilantes to exterminate anyone with real or imagined ties to the Left. Between 500,000 and over one million Indonesians were slaughtered, often hacked to death with machetes at night and dumped into the Brantas and Solo rivers until local officials complained that corpses were damming the irrigation weirs. Hundreds of thousands more were cast without trial as Tapol (political prisoners) into penal camps like Buru Island, among them Indonesia's greatest novelist, Pramoedya Ananta Toer. The PKI—the largest non-ruling communist party on earth—was erased in a single monsoon season.

With the Left annihilated, President Sukarno's balancing act collapsed. On March 11, 1966, with unidentified troops surrounding Merdeka Palace, Sukarno signed the Supersemar order transferring executive authority to restore order to Suharto. Suharto outlawed the PKI the next morning, purged the parliament and civil service, and by March 1967 had stripped the founding father of the presidency altogether. Sukarno died under house arrest at Wisma Yaso in June 1970, while atop a subterranean foundation of unacknowledged graves rose the rigid, corporatist pyramid of the New Order.

II. The Developmental State (1970s–1980s)

Suharto offered Indonesians a bargain stripped of any pretense of democracy: keep your mouths shut, and the regime will feed you. To make good on the economic half of it, he handed the macroeconomic levers of the state to a team of American-trained technocrats—Widjojo Nitisastro, Ali Wardhana, Mohammad Sadli, Emil Salim, and J.B. Sumarlin—mentored by Sumitro Djojohadikusumo and nicknamed the Berkeley Mafia. Simultaneously, starting in 1974, Suharto summoned a brilliant young aeronautical engineer named B.J. Habibie home from Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm in West Germany to spearhead an ambitious rival vision: state-led high-tech industrialization, anchored in the BPPT research agency and the IPTN aircraft plant in Bandung. Riding the windfalls of the 1973 and 1979 OPEC oil booms, five-year development plans (Repelita) paved highways, built village schools and clinics, and drove Indonesia to rice self-sufficiency by 1984.

The price of this development was a military and bureaucratic machine that metastasized through every organ of society. Under the doctrine of Dwifungsi (Dual Function), ABRI officers held reserved seats in parliament and ran provinces, regencies, and state enterprises like garrison commands. In 1973, the regime forcibly fused Indonesia's surviving political parties into two tame satellites—the Islamic PPP and the nationalist-Christian PDI—designed never to win, but merely to flank Golkar, the state's banyan-tree electoral machine. Required by compulsory 'monoloyalty' to vote yellow, civil servants and village heads delivered Golkar between 62% and 74% in six consecutive stage-managed elections from 1971 to 1997. Underneath the growth charts, a narrower circle gorged itself: military foundations, favored tycoons like Liem Sioe Liong, and above all Suharto's six children—the Cendana family—who turned toll roads, cloves, petrochemicals, television networks, and BULOG food imports into private family tollbooths.

III. The Cracks in the Edifice (1997-1998)

By 1997, the New Order miracle was hollow at the core. Indonesian banks and politically connected conglomerates had gorged on over $80 billion in unhedged short-term foreign debt on the assumption that Bank Indonesia's crawling peg would hold forever. Credit flowed not to solvent enterprises, but through KKN—Korupsi, Kolusi, dan Nepotisme—to anyone carrying a note from Jalan Cendana. When Thailand floated the baht on July 2, 1997, currency contagion tore across Southeast Asia. On August 14, Indonesia abandoned its currency band; within months, a rupiah that had traded at Rp 2,400 to the US dollar plunged toward Rp 16,800, vaporizing decades of middle-class savings and rendering virtually every major bank and conglomerate on the Jakarta Stock Exchange technically insolvent.

The policy response turned a financial panic into a social catastrophe. On November 1, 1997, sixteen private banks were abruptly closed under the first IMF program without deposit insurance, triggering terrified runs across the banking system. On January 15, 1998, Suharto signed a second Letter of Intent as IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus stood over him with arms folded—a photograph that instantly became a national emblem of humiliation. When Suharto named B.J. Habibie—whom foreign bondholders derided as a big-spending industrialist—as Vice President in March 1998 alongside a crony cabinet featuring his own daughter Tutut and timber tycoon Bob Hasan, the rupiah cratered anew. Inflation tore past 70%, millions lost their jobs, and when the government hiked fuel and electricity prices up to 70% on May 4 to satisfy the IMF, the New Order's thirty-year survival bargain—obedience in exchange for rice and stability—shattered for good.

IV. The Fall (May 1998)

University campuses had been marching under the banner of Reformasi for months, demanding an end to KKN, the repeal of Dwifungsi, and Suharto's resignation, when the spark that burned down the regime was struck on May 12, 1998. More than six thousand students at Trisakti University in West Jakarta had gathered for a peaceful march toward parliament; blocked by a police cordon along Jalan S. Parman, they agreed late that afternoon to retreat back inside their campus gates. As the students turned to walk back, security forces on the ground and snipers positioned on the surrounding pedestrian overpasses opened fire with live ammunition into the retreating crowd. Four unarmed students were killed—Elang Mulia Lesmana, Hery Hartanto, Hafidin Royan, and Hendriawan Sie—and dozens more were wounded. Photographs of their blood pooling on the Trisakti pavement detonated the capital.

What followed from May 13 to May 15 was both a spontaneous explosion of urban fury and a chillingly orchestrated pogrom. Across Jakarta, Medan, and Surakarta, mobs—some local, others trucked in by organized provocateurs with cropped hair and military boots—torched over 4,000 shops, banks, and homes, disproportionately targeting ethnic Chinese Indonesians who had been scapegoated for the economic collapse. Over a thousand people died in Jakarta alone, many burned alive inside locked shopping malls, while human rights volunteers led by Father Sandyawan Sumardi documented the systematic gang rape and assault of well over a hundred Chinese Indonesian women and girls.

On May 18, tens of thousands of students broke through the gates of the DPR/MPR complex in Senayan, swarming the green rooftop dome. That afternoon, Golkar DPR Speaker Harmoko stunned the nation by calling on Suharto to step down. On May 20, Amien Rais called off a million-person march at Monas only after tanks ringed the square, while fourteen economic ministers led by Ginandjar Kartasasmita refused to serve in Suharto's proposed reshuffle. Abandoned by his parliament, his cabinet, and finally told by Armed Forces Commander General Wiranto that the military could no longer hold the streets, Suharto appeared at Merdeka Palace at 9:00 AM on May 21, 1998, and read his resignation.

V. The Caretaker Regime (May 1998–October 1999)

Minutes after Suharto finished reading, Chief Justice Sarwata swore you in under Article 8 of the 1945 Constitution as the 3rd President of the Republic of Indonesia. Almost nobody in Jakarta expected you to last the month. To the students occupying Senayan, you were Suharto's devoted pupil—the man who had once called him 'SGS' (Super Genius Suharto). To the nationalist generals in Cilangkap, you were a civilian engineer who had used the Association of Indonesian Muslim Intellectuals (ICMI) to encroach on military procurement and politics. To currency traders in Singapore, you were 'Mr. Crack,' the man who wanted to build turboprops while the central bank was out of dollars.

Yet over the next twelve months, working eighteen-hour days at Merdeka Palace, your caretaker presidency unleashed a constitutional revolution. You opened the gates of Cipinang Prison for political prisoners from Sri Bintang Pamungkas and Muchtar Pakpahan to Xanana Gusmão. You abolished the SIUPP press censorship regime, ratified ILO labor conventions, separated the National Police from ABRI, enacted landmark Decentralization and Central Bank Independence statutes, and lifted the 48-party floodgates for the June 7, 1999 democratic election. In Aceh, you lifted DOM military rule and apologized in person for army atrocities; in East Timor, you stunned the world in January 1999 by offering a UN-administered ballot between special autonomy and independence.

Now it is June 1999, and every gamble is coming due at once. Megawati Sukarnoputri's PDI-P has won a 34% plurality in the election; your former ICMI ally Amien Rais is maneuvering to unite the Islamic parties behind Gus Dur; Akbar Tandjung holds Golkar's party machine at arm's length; General Wiranto's commanders are arming militias in East Timor; and a massive Rp 546 billion campaign slush-fund scandal at Bank Bali is about to detonate under your inner circle. In four months, 700 delegates will gather in Senayan to vote on your Accountability Speech. History remembers that Habibie lost that vote 355 to 322. Whether it turns out that way this time is in your hands.
